key_facts: Facial papules and pustules in a baby. **Comedones** = true acne; pustules without comedones = **cephalic pustulosis**.
Sebaceous glands driven by **maternal and neonatal androgens**, plus *Cutibacterium*.
Neonatal: **observe**, gentle cleansing. Infantile: **BPO ± topical retinoid**. No tetracyclines under 12.
Acne **between ages 1 and 6**, signs of hyperandrogenism, or nodular / scarring disease: refer.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Overactive sebaceous glands respond to **maternal and neonatal androgens**, with follicular *Cutibacterium* colonisation and the same plugging and inflammation cascade as later acne. Androgen drive falls after infancy and rises again at adrenarche, which is why **mid-childhood acne (ages 1–6) is very rare** and suggests an endocrine cause.

fig.caption: The same follicle steps as teenage acne: a plug forms, then inflammation. True acne needs comedones.

ul: **Neonatal:** comedones on the scalp, chest and back; inflammatory lesions on the cheeks, chin and forehead.
**Infantile:** mainly the cheeks; can be more inflammatory or nodular.

fig.caption: Neonatal acne: small papules and pustules on the cheeks, chin and forehead of a well baby, with a few tiny comedones. It is not caused by poor hygiene.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. If the age is atypical or the disease severe, look for accelerated growth, early sexual development or hirsutism. Refer mid-childhood or severe unresponsive acne to endocrinology.

ul: Look for fast growth, early puberty signs, hirsutism, body odour.
Mid-childhood or severe unresponsive acne → endocrinology.

ddx.name: Cephalic pustulosis
ddx.f: No or few comedones; may respond to topical antifungal.

ddx.name: Periorificial dermatitis
ddx.f: Around mouth and eyes; often steroid-related.

sections.title: Management
blocks: Usually **observe**. Gentle cleansing; avoid greasy, comedogenic products. Most cases clear without scarring.

ul: **Mild:** benzoyl peroxide ± topical retinoid (adapalene or tretinoin) as tolerated. Check the age licence.
**Moderate:** a topical regimen ± an age-appropriate oral **erythromycin**-class antibiotic. **Avoid tetracyclines under 12.**
**Severe, nodular or scarring:** refer to dermatology. Specialists do use isotretinoin in infants when indicated.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Suspected hyperandrogenism (accelerated growth, body odour, pubic hair, clitoromegaly).
Nodular or scarring disease, or treatment failure.

pearls: Reassure parents that neonatal acne is not caused by poor hygiene.
Do not use adult OTC acne kits on infants without checking age licences.
Persistent facial pustules in a neonate: consider cephalic pustulosis rather than true acne.

quiz.q: Neonatal vs infantile acne: age ranges?
quiz.a: Neonatal: birth to ~6 weeks. Infantile: ~6 weeks to 12–16 months.

quiz.q: Which oral antibiotic class to avoid under 12?

quiz.a: Very rare: look for hyperandrogenism and refer to endocrinology.
